claims.text: A machine-learned interatomic potential can be trained from a minimal set of ab initio molecular-dynamics snapshots spanning solid and liquid phases.
Thermodynamic integration or nested sampling performed with the trained potential can produce solid and liquid free energies up to melting.
The proposed workflow can accurately retain vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions to high-temperature free energies.
The trained potential will interpolate the ab initio potential-energy surfaces of both crystalline and molten states in multielement alloys with high fidelity.
Using a machine-learned potential makes extensive configurational sampling substantially cheaper than direct first-principles sampling.
The cheaper sampling will preserve near-first-principles accuracy for phase free energies.
First-principles calculations for multicomponent alloys have high computational demands.
The proposed workflow will reduce computational cost by approximately an order of magnitude relative to full ab initio molecular dynamics or complete TOR-TILD.
The workflow will match or closely approximate the accuracy of full ab initio molecular dynamics or TOR-TILD for melting properties and high-temperature thermal data.
The workflow can predict melting temperature, latent heat, fusion entropy, and high-temperature thermophysical properties.
The proposed applicability domain extends to alloys containing as many as five principal elements.
The proposed temperature domain extends from ambient temperature to near melting and encompasses solid–liquid coexistence.
Applicability is restricted to alloys without extreme chemical short-range order.
Accuracy depends on adequate sampling of composition and temperature in the training data.
Accuracy depends on whether structural features such as chemical short-range order are represented by the potential.
Errors greater than 5% in predicted melting temperature or latent heat relative to experiment or full ab initio references would falsify the hypothesis.
